newsitem.title: RWANDA: Lone doctor said aiding Zaire cholera victims.
newsitem.headline: Lone doctor said aiding Zaire cholera victims.

text.p: An Argentine doctor is battling alone to treat cholera sufferers among a huge mass of Rwandan Hutu refugees camped around a hillside town in eastern Zaire, his medical charity said on Wednesday.
Dr Abel Pasqualini estimates there are 250,000 refugees at the site.

Medicos en Catastrofe Internacional (Doctors in International Catastrophes) told Reuters their doctor was the only one reaching the makeshift camp at the small town of Mwenga, 80 km (50 miles) southwest of rebel-held Bukavu.

The agency, in radio contact from Rwanda with Pasqualini, said he saw men, women and children dying when he last visited Mwenga on Monday, where he said cholera was present. He was due to head back there on Wednesday.
"Our doctor saw dead people, he saw dying people and he saw many wounded and sick people," MCI spokesman Alesandro Rayces told Reuters in the Rwandan capital Kigali.

There was no separate confirmation of the report that nearly all the 300,000 refugees who had lived in camps near Bukavu, on the border with Rwanda, had marched off to Mwenga when fighting broke out between Zairean troops and Tutsi rebels.

The whereabouts of the Bukavu area refugees had been unknown. Many were thought to have melted into the surrounding hills. If the doctor's estimates are correct, it would mean Mwenga is home to more than a fifth of all the refugees affected by the fighting which erupted a month ago in eastern Zaire.
Hutu militiamen responsible for the 1994 genocide of some 800,000 minority Tutsis in Rwanda have controlled the refugee camps since they were set up in Zaire when Hutus fled a victorious Tutsi army.
Rayces said Pasqualini had worked in Bukavu before the rebels seized it and managed to cross the front lines to Mwenga because of good contacts with soldiers on both sides.
"He cannot cope on his own. He has to attend to Bukavu hospital as well as Mwenga. It is too much, we need help in there and we need it yesterday," Rayces said.

"Every day we wait, it is more people dying, more sick people getting worse. These people have lost their body defence systems and a disease like cholera just takes them away without a fight," he added.

Rayces said many refugees were being held hostage by the former Rwandan Hutu soldiers but said some were also genuinely afraid of going back home for fear of reprisals for their role in the genocide that many took part in.
Up to 400,000 refugees are believed to be without any aid in Mugunga camp, further north near the border town of Goma.
Cholera, often spread by contaminated water, killed at least 30,000 refugees within weeks after more than one million Hutus fled from Rwanda into eastern Zaire in 1994 after the genocide.
